\chapter{Eye, Ear, Mouth, and Nose}
\label{ch:pa-face-parts}
\hlchaptermodality{12}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the eye, ear, mouth, and nose in Punjabi, tell a doubled consonant that survived from one that vanished into tone, and clear up the false friend \pa{ਕੰਨ} shares in spelling, but not in root, with \pa{ਕਰਨਾ}.}

The chapter closes on \pa{ਨੱਕ}, completing the face: the reader produces \pa{ਅੱਖ}, \pa{ਕੰਨ}, \pa{ਮੂੰਹ} and \pa{ਨੱਕ}, names \pa{ਅੱਖ} and \pa{ਨੱਕ} as unbroken PIE cousins of eye and nose that kept their doubled consonants and so never traded a sound for a tone, and states that \pa{ਮੂੰਹ} alone among the four carries a level high tone, the same one first heard in \pa{ਚਾਹ}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[akkh]{\pa{ਅੱਖ} — the eye that kept both its consonants}

\label{lesson:PA-C12-akkh}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਭੈਣ}} closed a chapter about people. This chapter checks on how someone \emph{is} — starting with the parts of the body a friend might actually ask about.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਅੱਖ}} — \emph{akkh} — \textbf{eye}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਅ}}, the bare vowel-carrier for \emph{a}, then the \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} \emph{addak} — the same doubling mark from \textbf{\pa{ਰੱਬ}} and \textbf{\pa{ਦੁੱਧ}} — over \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} \emph{kh}. Read together: \emph{a-kkh}, the \emph{k} held and released with real force, not a tone standing in for it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{akkh} is inherited from Prakrit \textbf{akkhi}, from Sanskrit \textbf{akṣi}, \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} from Proto-Indo-Iranian *\emph{Hákši}, from Proto-Indo-European *\emph{h\textsubscript{3}ók\textsuperscript{w}s} — unbroken all the way to English \textbf{eye} itself.

Every tone you have met so far came from a consonant that \textbf{lost} something — its breathy voice, or the whole of itself. \textbf{\pa{ਖ}} here loses nothing: Sanskrit \emph{akṣi}'s consonant cluster became a \textbf{doubled} \emph{kkh} in Middle Indo-Aryan, and Punjabi still says both halves in full. That is exactly why \emph{akkh} is flat — the addak mark you are reading is the opposite move from a tone mark: it doubles a sound that survives, where a lost sound is what leaves a tone behind. Hindi took a different road with the same word, smoothing the cluster down into a nasal vowel, \emph{āṅkh} — no doubling, no tone, a third outcome entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{akkh} — eye — the \emph{kkh} held, not a tone
  \item \emph{Trace it:} PIE \emph{h\textsubscript{3}ók\textsuperscript{w}s} $\to$ Sanskrit \emph{akṣi} $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਅੱਖ}}, and $\to$ English \textbf{eye}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} a doubled consonant that survives (\emph{akkh}) against one that vanished into tone (\emph{bharā}'s \emph{bh})
  \item \emph{Name:} two other words that used the addak mark
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}eye.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Akkh}.) Which English word is the same word by unbroken descent? (\textbf{Eye}.) Does \emph{akkh} carry a tone? (\textbf{No} — its doubled \emph{kkh} survived in full, unlike a consonant that lost its breath.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%85\%E0\%A9\%B1\%E0\%A8\%96}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਅੱਖ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%85\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%B7\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit akṣi}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kann]{\pa{ਕੰਨ} — a false friend hiding in plain sight}

\label{lesson:PA-C12-kann}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{madad karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do a favour of help,\textquotedblright{} and pull its stem apart: \textbf{kar-}. Watch that same string of sounds turn up again, meaning something it has nothing to do with.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੰਨ}} — \emph{kann} — \textbf{ear}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਕ}} \emph{k}, \textbf{\pa{ੰ}} the \emph{ṭippī} nasal, \textbf{\pa{ਨ}} \emph{n} — and the vowel is nasalized where \textbf{\pa{ਅੱਖ}} doubled a consonant instead. \emph{Ka-nn}, with the doubling this time carried by the nasal mark rather than the addak.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਕੰਨ}} is inherited from Sanskrit \textbf{karṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} Its own root beyond Sanskrit has never been securely traced — one guess ties it to a word for \textquotedblleft{}twisting\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}winding,\textquotedblright{} another to a word for \textquotedblleft{}point,\textquotedblright{} and no source picks a winner.

Here is the trap: \textbf{karṇa} looks exactly like it is hiding \textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}} \emph{karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} the very verb inside \textbf{\pa{ਮਦਦ} \pa{ਕਰਨਾ}}. It is not. \emph{Karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do,\textquotedblright{} traces to a completely different Proto-Indo-European root, *\emph{k\textsuperscript{w}er-}. \emph{Karṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}ear,\textquotedblright{} does not connect to it at all — the resemblance is a coincidence of sound, the kind every language accumulates, and Punjabi keeps both words close enough in spelling that a learner has to be told, not left to guess.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kann} — ear
  \item \emph{State:} is \emph{kann} related to \emph{karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}? (No — a coincidence of sound.)
  \item \emph{Run through:} \textbf{akkh}, \textbf{kann} — eye, ear
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{madad karnā}'s own \textbf{kar-}, and how it differs from \emph{kann}'s
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Kann}.) Does it share a root with \emph{karnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — different Proto-Indo-European roots entirely.) Name the two body words so far. (\emph{Akkh}, \emph{kann}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%95\%E0\%A9\%B0\%E0\%A8\%A8}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਕੰਨ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%A3}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit karṇa}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūnh]{\pa{ਮੂੰਹ} — a consonant that wore all the way down to a tone}

\label{lesson:PA-C12-munh}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਚਾਹ}}'s final \textbf{\pa{ਹ}} was not really a consonant — it marked a level high tone, because the word ended right there. This word ends the same way, from a consonant that used to be something else entirely. And unlike \textbf{\pa{ਕੰਨ}}, which only \emph{looks} like it hides \textbf{\pa{ਕਰਨਾ}} inside it, this word hides no false friend at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਮੂੰਹ}} — \emph{mūnh} — \textbf{mouth}, also \textbf{face}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਮ}} \emph{m}, \textbf{\pa{ੂ}} long \emph{ū}, \textbf{\pa{ੰ}} the nasal \emph{ṭippī}, \textbf{\pa{ਹ}} — again not spoken as \emph{h}, marking the same level high tone you first read in \textbf{\pa{ਚਾਹ}}: \emph{mū́h̃}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mūnh} is inherited from Sanskrit \textbf{mukha}, \textquotedblleft{}face, mouth\textquotedblright{} — Punjabi also kept the same word a second time, whole, as the learned borrowing \textbf{\pa{ਮੁਖ}} \emph{mukh}, the way it kept both \emph{\pa{ਪਸੰਦ}} and its own inherited relatives side by side before.

On the inherited path, \emph{mukha}'s middle \textbf{kh} did not simply vanish. Middle Indo-Aryan first softened intervocalic \emph{kh} down to a plain \textbf{h} — a regular, well-worn move, nothing to do with the breathy-voiced letters that gave you \emph{bharā}'s low tone or \emph{samajhṇā}'s falling one. Punjabi then lost \textbf{that} \emph{h} too, the same way it lost \emph{cāh}'s Persian-final one, and let its pitch land on the vowel before it: level and high, because — exactly as in \emph{cāh} — nothing follows it in the word.

So \emph{mūnh} and \emph{cāh} reach a level high tone from different histories — one from a worn-down \emph{kh}, one from a borrowed word's own \emph{h} — and arrive at the identical sound.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{mūnh} — mouth, face — level and high
  \item \emph{Match:} \emph{mūnh}'s tone against \emph{cāh}'s
  \item \emph{Trace it:} Sanskrit \emph{mukha} $\to$ \emph{kh} softens to \emph{h} $\to$ \emph{h} is lost $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਮੂੰਹ}}
  \item \emph{Name:} the learned twin of \emph{mūnh} that kept the whole word intact
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tone does \emph{mūnh} carry, and which earlier word — not a body word, but the same pattern — first showed it? (\textbf{Level high}; \textbf{cāh}, tea, from Chapter 10.) What softened before Punjabi lost it entirely in \emph{mukha} $\to$ \emph{mūnh}? (\textbf{Kh}, first to plain \textbf{h}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%AE\%E0\%A9\%82\%E0\%A9\%B0\%E0\%A8\%B9}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਮੂੰਹ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%96}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit mukha}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nakk]{\pa{ਨੱਕ} — the whole face, run back}

\label{lesson:PA-C12-nakk}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਅੱਖ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਕੰਨ}}, \textbf{\pa{ਮੂੰਹ}} — eye, ear, mouth. One more completes the face, and it closes the chapter on the cleanest English cousin this book has found yet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਨੱਕ}} — \emph{nakk} — \textbf{nose}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\pa{ਨ}} \emph{n}, \textbf{\pa{ੱ}} the addak, \textbf{\pa{ਕ}} \emph{k} — the same doubling mark as \textbf{\pa{ਅੱਖ}}, and for the same reason: nothing here was ever breathy, so nothing here traded itself for a tone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nakk} is inherited from Old Punjabi \textbf{naku}, and its root is Proto-Indo- European *\emph{neh\textsubscript{2}s-} — unbroken, all the way to English \textbf{nose} itself, Latin \emph{nāsus}, and Lithuanian \emph{nósis}. Like \emph{akkh}, \emph{nakk} needed no ship and no loanword to reach you, only the ordinary work of sound change and a doubled consonant that held its ground.

Run the whole face and its tone table: \textbf{akkh} flat, doubled; \textbf{kann} flat, nasal, no relation at all to \emph{karnā}; \textbf{mūnh} level and high, a worn-down \emph{kh}; \textbf{nakk} flat, doubled, the clean cousin of \emph{nose}. Two of the four carry no tone because their old consonants survived whole; one carries a level high tone because its consonant vanished entirely; none of the four carries the low or falling tones you met on verbs and on \emph{bharā} — those belong to words that opened or closed with a breathy voice, and nothing here ever did.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four face words — \textbf{akkh}, \textbf{kann}, \textbf{mūnh}, \textbf{nakk}
  \item \emph{Trace it:} PIE \emph{neh\textsubscript{2}s-} $\to$ \textbf{\pa{ਨੱਕ}}, and $\to$ English \textbf{nose}
  \item \emph{Sort:} which of the four carry a tone, and which do not
  \item \emph{Name:} the doubled-consonant pair, \textbf{akkh} and \textbf{nakk}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}nose.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nakk}.) Which English word is the same word by unbroken descent? (\textbf{Nose}.) Name the four face words and which one carries a tone. (\emph{Akkh}, \emph{kann}, \emph{mūnh}, \emph{nakk}; only \emph{mūnh}, level and high.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A8\%A8\%E0\%A9\%B1\%E0\%A8\%95}{Wiktionary: \pa{ਨੱਕ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
